# jupycost

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/Openscapes/jupycost/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Openscapes/jupycost/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

jupycost provides functions for Openscapes to query and monitor patterns of usage and costs of the [JupyterHubs](https://openscapes.cloud) that we adminster in partnership with [2i2c](https://2i2c.org).

We monitor usage by querying a Prometheus time-series database, as well as the AWS Cost-Explorer API. jupycost allows us to do automated periodic reporting of usage. We also use Grafana to monitor usage interactively.

## Installation

You can install the development version of jupycost from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("Openscapes/jupycost")
```

## Authentication

Openscapes runs two hubs, each with its own Grafana instance and AWS account:

| Hub | `cluster` | Grafana URL |
|----|----|----|
| NASA | `"openscapeshub"` | <https://grafana.openscapes.2i2c.cloud> (the default `grafana_url`) |
| NMFS | `"nmfs-openscapes"` | <https://grafana.nmfs-openscapes.2i2c.cloud> |

jupycost reads credentials for the hub you are working with from these environment variables:

- `GRAFANA_TOKEN`, used by the Prometheus usage functions.
- `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and `AWS_REGION` (`us-east-1`), used by the cost and credit functions.

Cost functions don't take a credential argument, so they report on whichever AWS account the variables point to.
Make sure they match the `cluster` you ask for.
Prometheus functions use the token for the Grafana instance in `grafana_url`, so pass `grafana_url` explicitly for NMFS.

### Getting the credentials

**Grafana token**

1. Log in to the hub's Grafana instance (see the table above) as an admin.
2. Go to *Administration > Users and access > Service accounts*.
3. Create a service account (the Viewer role is enough), then choose *Add service account token*.
4. Copy the token right away, as it is only shown once.

**AWS credentials**

1. In the hub's AWS account, open *IAM* and create (or select) a user that can use Cost Explorer.
   The credit functions additionally call the AWS Billing credits API and look up the account ID through STS.
2. On the *Security credentials* tab, choose *Create access key*.
3. Copy the access key ID and secret access key.

### Saving the environment variables

Store the variables in your user-level `.Renviron` file so that R loads them at startup and they stay out of the project.
Open the file with:

``` r
usethis::edit_r_environ()
```

Because there are two hubs, the simplest approach is to save both sets with a prefix, which is also what the package test infrastructure expects:

``` sh
NASA_GRAFANA_TOKEN=<token>
NASA_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<key-id>
NASA_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<secret>
NMFS_GRAFANA_TOKEN=<token>
NMFS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<key-id>
NMFS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<secret>
```

Save the file and restart R.
Then, to work with one hub, use `set_env_vars()` to copy its variables to the unprefixed names the functions read (and set `AWS_REGION`):

``` r
library(jupycost)

set_env_vars("nmfs")
get_daily_usage_costs(cluster = "nmfs-openscapes")
```

In a function or a test, the original values are restored when it exits.
At the console, run `withr::deferred_run()` to restore them, or call `set_env_vars()` again for the other hub.

If you only work with one hub, you can instead save the unprefixed names directly.

### Tests and CI

Tests that hit Grafana or AWS use `set_env_vars()` to read the prefixed variables and are skipped when they are missing, so you can run the test suite without credentials.
On GitHub Actions the same variables are provided from repository secrets of the same names (for example `NASA_GRAFANA_TOKEN`), which is also where to put them for any automated reporting.
Never commit credential values to version control.
